newsitem.title: UK: British Millennium project to go ahead.
newsitem.headline: British Millennium project to go ahead.

text.p: Britain's plans to celebrate the Millennium with an exhibition in a giant dome on the banks of the River Thames were given the go-ahead on Thursday but doubts remained over how the project would be funded.
The Millennium Commission said it confirmed its decision to proceed with the exhibition at Greenwich, east London.
"The commission is now finalising the means by which the exhibition will be delivered within an acceptable budget," the commission said in a statement.
The funding of the project has been a recurring cause for worry with few potential sponsors giving their backing.
Doubts about the ambitious project surfaced on Wednesday when the opposition Labour Party voiced concerns about costs.

Millennium Central, the group overseeing the project, wants Labour's backing because the party is opinion poll favourite to win the next general election, due by May 1997, and money from the state lottery is needed for the scheme.
Labour's National Heritage spokesman, Jack Cunningham, reiterated his party's support for the exhibition but said Labour could not agree to give the organisers a blank cheque.
"Whilst I want to see the project proceed, I cannot agree to unlimited further expenditure on it," he said in a letter to National Heritage minister Virginia Bottomley.
Bottomley met the Millennium Commission on Wednesday to study the business plan put forward by Millennium Central.

The Commission is responsible for allocating funds from the National Lottery to Millennium events. Millennium Central wants 200 million poundsfrom the Lottery with another 150 million coming from the private sector and the rest from gate receipts, sponsorship and other sources.
But exactly how much extra is needed, and what the final bill for the lottery might be, remain uncertain.
Estimates of the cost of the exhibition vary widely from 350 million pounds to one billion pounds. The plan to be put to the Commission meeting settles on a figure of 704 million pounds.

The exhibition is planned to open on December 31, 1999, and last a year. Its central theme is time -- Greenwich is the home of the Meridian line that measures longitude around the globe, and clocks around the world are set from Greenwich Mean Time.
The dome, with glass sides and a white fabric roof supported by 12 giant masts, would cover 80,000 square metres and could comfortably house London's Trafalgar Square, including Nelson's Column.
